definition: Vex means to annoy or irritate.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word vex. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know vex should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The conference line's half-second echo vexed the negotiators into talking over one another for an hour.
Bother is milder than vex — a fly at the picnic, shooed and forgotten.
Infuriate is far stronger than vex: vexation prickles at your patience, while fury has already burned through it.

To irk is to rub someone the wrong way, quietly — a low-grade annoyance the irked person may never even mention. To vex is a shade sharper and far more persistent: a vexation keeps buzzing at the patience and insists on being noticed. An irked person shrugs; a vexed one mutters.

To nettle is to sting someone's pride just enough to redden the temper — usually one sharp, personal poke, often a remark. To vex is less personal and more patient: small irritations, delays, and riddles that nag at the attention over time. Nettle stings once; vexation keeps buzzing.
to smooth irritation away
to give simple satisfaction
Latin vexare produced vex and its own noun vexation, and then stopped; no other common English word shares the root. The similar-sounding convex is unrelated — it comes from vehere, 'to carry.'
Vex means to annoy or irritate.
The hotel's key cards vexed Mr.
Osei all weekend — accepted at midnight, refused at one, and at two, inexplicably, his room-service menu opened the door.
Vex is old, small, and precise: a vexation buzzes at your patience without breaking it.
The word can also color puzzles — a vexed question is one that nags — but the center is minor, persistent irritation.
When patience actually gives out, this unit's exasperate is waiting.
Vex suits small, persistent irritations and the faintly old-fashioned sentence — squeaks, delays, riddles that nag.
Annoy is the plain modern word; irk and nettle are its quieter cousins.
When the irritation has worn patience through, reach for this unit's exasperate instead.

The new oven at Solano's bakery worked perfectly except for one thing: its timer ran forty seconds slow.
Forty seconds is nothing, the salesman said.
But the discrepancy began to vex Marta within a week.

It was too small to justify a service call and too large to ignore; every batch asked her to choose between trusting the dial and trusting her wristwatch, and she caught herself muttering the difference under her breath while frosting cakes.
Her assistant shrugged at it.
The timer buzzed at the wrong moment forty times a day, and forty times a day she noticed.
In the end she taped a card over the display -- out of sight, out of argument -- and the muttering stopped.
